title: MTR Foods Bets on Quick Commerce, Clean Labels and a Viral Sambar Anthem
excerpt: The 102-year-old Karnataka brand is pairing heritage marketing with digital distribution to expand nationally, while a folk-fusion 'Sambar Anthem' racks up nearly 8 million YouTube views.
body:
• MTR Foods has launched a viral 'Sambar Anthem' campaign with folk-fusion artist Vasu Dixit, drawing nearly 8 million YouTube views since its July 4 debut in Bengaluru.
  • Digital commerce now accounts for close to 9% of parent company Orkla India's sales, with quick commerce becoming a key distribution engine for MTR beyond its southern strongholds.
  • The brand's new Prakriti range of premium, single-source spices targets younger consumers who scrutinise ingredient labels for preservatives and artificial additives.
  • MTR holds roughly 67.5% retail outlet presence in Karnataka and penetrates close to 90% of households in the state.

MTR Foods, the Bengaluru-headquartered packaged foods company founded in 1924, is executing a multi-front growth strategy that blends regional cultural marketing with digital-first distribution and clean-label product innovation. At the centre of its latest push is an unlikely marketing vehicle: a folk song about sambar.

The company's Sambar Anthem campaign, launched on July 4 in collaboration with folk-fusion musician Vasu Dixit, began not with a television spot but a morning concert at Cubbon Park in Bengaluru. MTR invited consumers online to share personal memories and emotions tied to sambar, then wove those responses into the lyrics of an original composition performed live for the first time at the event. The one-minute-44-second anthem has since amassed nearly 8 million views on YouTube and expanded across television, Spotify, radio and digital platforms, with outdoor advertising to follow.

"The soul of Karnataka food is sambar. If I say the word sambar to you, the first thought that comes into your mind is the taste of your mom's sambar, because sambar tastes different in different households."

— Anupam Nair, CMO and Growth Officer, MTR Foods

From Awareness to Availability

Behind the cultural campaign lies a fundamental strategic shift. According to Nair, MTR's growth engine is no longer primarily advertising — it is availability. The 102-year-old brand commands deep equity in southern India, sitting in roughly 67.5% of retail outlets in Karnataka and reaching close to 90% of households. But the real opportunity, Nair argues, lies in making MTR accessible wherever and however consumers choose to shop.

Digital commerce now contributes between 8.5% and 9% of sales for Orkla India, MTR's Norwegian parent company, and the figure is growing rapidly. Quick commerce platforms have been particularly transformative. In some categories — particularly fresh idli and dosa batter in Bengaluru — rapid delivery accounts for the bulk of sales. The platforms have also opened up markets MTR previously struggled to reach through traditional distribution.

"Even in a smaller town in Punjab or UP, now I can sell idli and dosa mix very easily," Nair told Social Samosa. "Earlier, it would have taken me a lot more effort to be able to be available there."

The Clean-Label Push

MTR is also responding to a pronounced shift in consumer behaviour around ingredients. Nair says shoppers — including those in tier-two towns — are now actively scrutinising product labels for preservatives, artificial colours, palm oil and trans fats before making purchase decisions.

The brand's most visible response is the Prakriti range, a premium, single-source spice portfolio launched to cater to ingredient-conscious consumers willing to pay more for quality. The range sources specific ingredients from the regions best known for cultivating them: Byadagi chillies from Karnataka, Araku turmeric from Andhra Pradesh and Kumbhraj coriander from Madhya Pradesh. Products are handpicked and produced in small batches to preserve natural oils and potency.

The company is also reimagining traditional dry formats into fresher, more convenient options. MTR's 3-Minute Breakfast range offers instant, no-cook meal solutions in cups and pouches, while sambar powder has been joined by fresh sambar paste in the portfolio.

"I can give them the healthiest product in the world, but if it doesn't taste well, it won't move."

— Anupam Nair, CMO and Growth Officer, MTR Foods

A Contested Market

MTR operates in a fiercely competitive landscape. Parent company Orkla India leads the Karnataka packaged spices market with a 31.2% share, according to CNBC-TV18, and also owns Eastern, which dominates in Kerala with roughly 70.4% retail outlet presence. But the category is crowded with regional brands like iD Fresh Food, Aachi, Brahmins, Sakthi and numerous unorganised local players.

The blended spices segment — which includes sambar masala — is projected to grow from 34% to 38% of the overall spice market by fiscal 2029, according to Orkla India data. That growth explains why MTR is investing heavily in retaining its regional base while expanding nationally through convenience categories like breakfast mixes and festive sweets.

What's Next

MTR's roadmap for the remainder of 2026 follows a familiar seasonal rhythm. The sambar push will continue through the coming months before the company pivots to festive staples — gulab jamun mix and Mysore Pak — ahead of Diwali.

Nationally, the brand sees quick commerce as the bridge between its South Indian roots and the rest of the country. Products like idli and dosa mixes are finding growing demand as South Indian cuisine gains broader acceptance, and rapid delivery ensures consumers who moved away from the South or developed a taste for the cuisine can access authentic products on demand.

For MTR, the challenge is executing this expansion without diluting the regional identity that built its brand. "You have to be honest to who you are," Nair said. "The consumer sees through you."
image_caption: A pot of vegetable sambar, the South Indian lentil dish at the heart of MTR's latest marketing campaign. The 102-year-old brand's viral 'Sambar Anthem' has drawn nearly 8 million YouTube views since launching in early July.
nri_angle: Quick commerce platforms are making MTR's South Indian products accessible to consumers nationwide, including diaspora communities who moved away from the South and seek authentic regional food on demand.
author: Diaspora Desk
